lines.text: Forty of the dead. One of you.
The only way out is in, so you run into the mine.
They follow you in.
Twenty metres in, the daylight's gone. And they stop.
The dead can't see in the dark.
When you die, your eyes dry out and go milky, like frosted glass.
In daylight, they see shapes. In the dark, nothing.
So you switch off your lamp, one hand on the rail.
A hundred metres down. Two hundred.
Then, far below, a green light.
Your hideout. A refuge chamber, built for trapped miners.
The mine shut twelve years ago. You fixed it up alone. Nobody knows it's here.
You come in through an airlock. The air inside is pushed a little harder, so bad air stays out.
Food. Six hundred ration packs. Two a day. Ten months.
Water. The rock drips forty litres a day.
Power. A turbine in the stream, and a wall of batteries.
A first aid kit. And a pickaxe by the door.
Your air comes down one shaft, three hundred metres.
A big fan at the top pushes it down.
Your turbine could never spin it. It runs on the line from the dam, three kilometres up the valley.
Nobody's there. It just keeps turning.
One rule down here. Never go up by day.
After weeks in the dark, your pupils open wide.
Step into sunlight, and you're almost blind for a minute.
A minute is all they need.
The only safe way up is at night. Three hundred metres of ladder. Two hours, in the dark.
Day one. The camera at the top shows the yard, full of them.
Day five. They're still there.
Day ten. They haven't moved.
At night they circle the shaft, staring down into the dark.
Day fourteen. At noon, the fan stops.
The air goes still.
You planned for everything. Food. Water. Power.
But you forgot one thing. Your air was never yours.
Without the fan, the air goes stale. Six days. Maybe seven.
That night, the radio crackles.
Someone is at the dam. A family, switching off every line they think is dead.
They don't know you exist.
One call, and they'd switch you back on.
Or you go up alone. There's an old second shaft, capped with steel.
Open it, and the mine breathes on its own. Cold air in, warm air out.
Two hours of ladder. Then six hundred metres across the yard.
Through them.
Do you call the dam, and tell strangers where you hide?
Or climb up alone, into the dead? Comment call, or alone.
